items.title: Otters appear to have declined throughout Ireland amid increased pressures on water quality, but remain ubiquitous
items.summary: Abstract Governments must report on the conservation status of species designated as protected. We assessed changes in the Near Threatened Eurasian otter Lutra lutra population throughout Ireland (the whole island) from the 1980s to the 2020s using four National Otter Surveys (6,060 sites surveyed) and citizen science data (10,980 records). In 2023–2024, otters were recorded at 65% (95% CI 62–68%) of sites in the Republic of Ireland and 66% (95% CI 58–74%) of sites in Northern Ireland. Rivers, lakes and coasts were included in the surveys. Long-term trends in the population estimate indicate a decline of 24−27% (or 3−18% after correction for negative methodological biases). Short-term trends indicated changes of −7% to +2% in the Republic of Ireland and −26% to −27% in Northern Ireland. items.title: Engaging Primary School Children in Environmental Education Through Citizen Science
items.summary: This dissertation examines approaches to supporting Environmental Education (EE) by engaging primary school pupils in Citizen Science (CS) focused on freshwater conservation. In response to the decline in water quality in Ireland, the study compares two methods: a traditional paper-based approach and a digital approach using a mobile app designed to assist with macroinvertebrate-based water quality monitoring. The research explores how these approaches influence pupils’ engagement and self-efficacy in participating in CS. A quasi-experimental study was carried out in three Irish primary schools, with experimental groups using the app and control groups using paper-based methods. The workshops combined classroom learning with practical activities involving the identification of live macroinvertebrates, enabling pupils to explore their local ecosystems as citizen scientists. items.title: Empowering Communities: How Citizen Science Transforms Water Monitoring
items.summary: Citizen science has been increasingly adopted in research projects monitoring the ecological status of aquatic ecosystems and assessing pollutants across water resources. In the past years, the DCU Water Institute has hosted a number of projects that involve the general public in collecting environmental data in Irish freshwater environments. We present here an overview of these projects, detailing their scope, timeline, progress, and the citizen science activities conducted. These projects have investigated nutrient excess, visible signs of pollution, macroinvertebrate diversity, and emerging pollutants of concern, targeting either specific catchment areas or waterbodies throughout the whole country. items.summary: Citizen science can considerably assist researchers in collecting environmental data, expanding the scope of projects and serving an educational purpose. This framework was utilized for establishing the surveying methodology, recruiting our volunteers, training them as citizen scientists, engaging and supporting them during the data collection, and communicating results. items.title: Trends and purposes of European river monitoring and restoration
items.summary: This study provides the first geospatial analysis of the trends and uptake of European river monitoring and restoration. European monitoring targets rivers draining agricultural and urban land, which leads to geospatial biases due to the co-occurrence with soils, topography, and river orders. Most notably, intermittent rivers and ephemeral streams are underrepresented due to lower monitoring intensities in Southern Europe, headwaters, and catchments with steeper slopes or less arable soils. Improving monitoring efforts in these ecosystems can advance our scientific understanding of complex linkages between ecological quality outcomes and specific stressors. items.summary: This research evaluates water quality in two contrasting hydro-climatic regions: the River Liffey in Ireland and the Andarax River in Spain. items.title: Drought impacts on river water temperature: A process‐based understanding from temperate climates
items.summary: Abstract High river water temperature (Tw) extremes have been widely reported during drought conditions as extreme low‐flows often coincide with high atmospheric energy inputs. This has significant implications for freshwater ecosystem health and sustainable river management practices globally. items.title: Assessing the impact of COVID-19 lockdown on surface water quality in Ireland using advanced Irish water quality index (IEWQI) model
items.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly impacted various aspects of life, including environmental conditions. Surface water quality (WQ) is one area affected by lockdowns imposed to control the virus's spread. Numerous recent studies have revealed the considerable impact of COVID-19 lockdowns on surface WQ. In response, this research aimed to assess the impact of COVID-19 lockdowns on surface water quality in Ireland using an advanced WQ model. To achieve this goal, six years of water quality monitoring data from 2017 to 2022 were collected for nine water quality indicators in Cork Harbour, Ireland, before, during, and after the lockdowns.
